title: 👾 The AI trade’s quarterly checkup
body_text: New York City had an electric summer following the Knicks victory in the NBA Finals, and that sweet victory was enjoyed by basically everyone, with a few exceptions. One of those exceptions is “people who work for New York Knicks owner James Dolan.” When and how you have heard about the eccentric billionaire cable heir depends on which incredibly weird or petty thing Dolan did that made its way into your feed, from siccing facial recognition technology on perceived adversaries to making his vanity project band, JD & The Straight Shot, the de facto opening act for major stars playing at Madison Square Garden. Still, a new report from The Athletic may take the cake for Dolan lore, as evidently when employees of the Knicks had been eagerly awaiting details on their eligibility for sought-after NBA Champions rings, Dolan insisted that IT send out a phishing test email purporting to offer everyone in the organization a free ring, with the people who clicked on the included link getting not a Knicks ‘26 ring but instead a mandatory cyber-security seminar. The nice thing about business news is that it’s essentially the only category where the subjects legally have to be honest with you at least four times per year (or half that often in Europe). This week we’ll get a look past the bluster, the boasting, the rumors, and the suspicions about what’s actually happening with the AI trade, with companies representing the entire AI behemoth snout-to-tail reporting earnings. The big three are the hyperscalers, the companies that have existing cloud operations and ambitions to supplement those with large AI capital investments: Alphabet , Amazon , and Microsoft . Yes, all of them have their ancillary business that could be megacorps in their own right — Microsoft with its Office and video game divisions (and don’t forget LinkedIn!), Alphabet with its advertising and phone business, and Amazon with its retail operation — but realistically investors are going to be paying attention to their AI buildout, how much it’s costing, the manner in which they intend to cover those costs, and so on. Those costs are other companies’ sales, and we’ll be hearing a lot from them, too. If you want to build an AI data center (and these guys really, really do!) you’ve got to spend money that eventually ends up in the pockets of the disk storage companies ( Sandisk and Seagate are both reporting), the chip manufacturers ( Intel on Thursday, AMD the following week) and the companies that make optical communications equipment ( Corning , on Tuesday) and power and cooling racks ( Vertiv, on Wednesday). Those are just the direct suppliers, but you’ve got to build the things too, and for that you need power generation ( GE Vernova reports Wednesday) and the equipment to construct the things ( Caterpillar , the day after) The long and short of it is that this week will be a check-up on virtually every component of the most important trade in markets. Traders will be making inferences based on these flagship companies for not just the rest of earnings season and their competitors, but also the overall health of the trade itself. The AI trade in general and semiconductors in particular have been rattled for the past few weeks, as my colleague Luke Kawa wrote in EntryPoint last Friday. The VanEck Semiconductor index has taken a beating over the past several months, with semis nearing a dip below the 200 day moving average that could spell algorithm-inflected pain for bulls. title: Netflix’s Indian summer
body_text: The days of playing a housekeeper at the Airbnb you already paid a cleaning fee for are over. As part of a new global policy effective Nov. 20, Airbnb hosts will not be able to ask guests to do chores that require “significant effort” such as taking out the trash, stripping the sheets, or washing dishes. Hosts can still ask guests to leave dishes in the sink or, say, leave the trash in a bear-proof container when staying in a cabin, but Airbnb has finally drawn the line between being a considerate guest and working for your keep, after already paying for it. Stocks had a particularly rough day on Thursday, with the S&P 500 falling 1.2% and the Nasdaq 100 dropping 2.6%, marking the tech-heavy index’s worst day since June. Despite posting a relatively strong third quarter where earnings came in above expectations and revenue landed roughly in line with estimates, Netflix has been sent lower this week after the streamer set a new Q4 sales forecast that was slimmer than Wall Street expected and tempered ad revenue estimates. One silver lining among the clouds looming over the company from its Q3 report? India, which got six shoutouts in Netflix’s latest letter to shareholders; double the amount of references to the “US” or “United States.” Clearly the streamer has something to shout about in the Indian market, which sits in what is — currently, at least — the smallest global region for Netflix. India sits in the company’s Asia Pacific region, which accounted for just $1.54 billion of its total $12.88 billion revenue figure from the third quarter. Still, the APAC segment’s position could change if the success in India continues, with Netflix adding more net paid subscribers in the nation than ever before, revenues rising 18%, and view hours up 24% from the same period last year. The streamer highlighted “Lock Upp,” its first daily reality TV show, as a standout success in India, driving “the most viewing of any title on Netflix” in the country ever. Scripted hits like “Operation Safed Sagar” and “Musafir Cafe” also contributed to growth, as the company itself downsizes at a faster pace than it has since 2022. Doing better in the most populous nation in the world, which per the World Bank’s reckonings also still boasts one of the fastest growing major global economies, is obviously a boon for the world’s biggest film and TV streaming service. However, with at least some of the growth undoubtedly down to a generous tie-in with Indian e-commerce giant Flipkart — customers can get a free monthly Netflix Mobile subscription by spending ₹299 (~$3.15) on four individual orders in a single month — it might be a little early to put too much stock in the advance for now. According to the latest installment of an infrequent Gallup survey of US adults (the first since 2022), fewer of us are heading out to shop for groceries, eating out in restaurants, and even ordering takeout food, as the way Americans live week-to-week continues to shift. Gallup noted that Americans are tending to spread their weekly grocery trips out a little further, while also highlighting the rise of online staple shopping, with 15% of Americans now doing a weekly grocery order online compared to just 4% less than 10 years ago. Dining out and ordering takeout, despite the cursed online discourse around how it can sometimes work out cheaper than eating at home, have both declined of late. A still stunning — to this writer, at least — 4% of Americans still report that they never eat out at a restaurant. That — or 278 billion kroner, to be more accurate — is how much Norway’s sovereign wealth fund lost over the last quarter, the company that manages the fund announced yesterday . The loss was mostly owing to just how much of the world’s largest wealth fund’s fixed income portfolio is wrapped up in government bonds, with 70% allocated to the interest rate-hit investments. Staggeringly, shedding $30 billion doesn’t actually put too much of a dent in the Norwegian wealth fund, which is still worth around $2.3 trillion, shedding the rough equivalent of an Adidas ($31.5B), 7-Eleven ($30.5B), or Reddit ($29.5B) in a single quarter still has to sting. title: 👀 Wall Street gets a peak inside Anthropic
body_text: The Los Angeles Dodgers were favorites to win this year’s World Series. And when they were surprisingly swept by the Milwaukee Brewers, it wasn’t just the team that lost – businesses around Dodger stadium also saw potential revenue evaporate. Fortune reports that a restaurant group that runs bars near the stadium prepared for exactly that possibility by placing a $60,000 trade on Kalshi that the Dodgers would not advance. The trade, which doubled in value after LA’s playoff exit, helped to fill the hole in the group’s revenue from all the Dodger’s fans who now won’t be packing bars before or during World Series games. Investors have been eager to peek under the hood of Anthropic ahead of its anticipated Wall Street debut, which could value the AI company at around $2 trillion. The Wall Street Journal got their hands on an early draft of Anthropic’s hotly anticipated S-1 , which paints a picture of a company with surging revenues but also sky-high compute costs and a medley of risk factors. Here are some highlights : Revenue is growing at an impressive rate: It reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of this year, up from $1.1 billion in the same period a year earlier. They are also spending a ton of money on compute. The company spent $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, up from $2.3 billion spent on infrastructure during the same period in 2025. The company already agreed to pay $450 billion in cloud computing agreements over the next seven to ten years and it can’t back out of those. It warned it could potentially spend $750 billion “in the coming years,” per the Journal. It is in the red. The company reported a net loss of $80 billion during the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion a year earlier. Most of that loss is accounting charges; it still reported operating loss in H1 2026 but it was lower than the year before. Anthropic makes it very clear that it sees AI as a risky business. According to the Journal, “roughly a third” of the draft prospectus was dedicated to risk factors ranging from liability tied to potential data security incidents, models “blackmailing” people to the political risk tied to the backlash against data centers. The CEO isn’t getting a Musk-sized pay day. Dario Amodei’s total compensation is $18 million, which is in line with the median pay for S&P 500 companies but less than many of his Big Tech peers. Anthropic’s numbers scooped by the Journal give a rare glimpse at the precise economics of running an AI company. The good news is Anthropic’s revenue, as of June 30, is growing faster than its costs. The bad news is that its costs are really high. Anthropic needs to convince investors that its revenues are going to keep growing faster than its enormous spending commitments. But, as Bloomberg’s Parmy Olson recently pointed out , the price of building AI models keeps going up while the price tag on AI products keeps going down. Anthropic can't guarantee that its revenue will keep soaring, but it's already committed to paying hundreds of billions of dollars for computing power. “That doesn’t necessarily mean a bursting bubble, but it does look like the real power increasingly lies with the companies that distribute and power the technology: cloud giants like Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and Amazon .com Inc.,” Olson wrote. Amazon’s annual holiday hiring surge is set to be bigger than ever, the e-commerce giant has announced . The company says it will hire over 300,000 seasonal, part-time, and full-time new employees to deal with the increase in orders it sees during the holiday shopping season. The yield on 10-year French government bonds hit 5% on Wednesday , as the nation’s borrowing costs spiked amid mass unrest that has turned violent at times. Larry Ellison went on a borrowing spree to fund his son’s takeover of Warner Bros ., the Wall Street Journal reports . Wall Street stock strategists have a new favorite word . The average US mortgage rate fell for the first time in 2 months, dropping to 7.41% from 7.5% . Coca-Cola bought Costa coffee for $5 billion, hoping to create a global self-serve coffee behemoth. It didn’t end up that way, Bloomberg reports , largely because espresso machines are more complex than soda vending machines.
